title: Queering Basic Needs Work
abstract: ABSTRACT Rooted in practice, this article explores how gender and sexuality centers, queer and trans (QT) resource practitioners, and basic needs units and programs can “queer” basic needs work to better serve and support low‐income 2SLGBTQIA+ college students. Three practitioners from the University of Michigan Spectrum Center share their approach to meeting the basic needs of QT students and how practitioners must endeavor to meet the similar, pronounced, and unique needs of this population of students.

title: Beyond Tuition: How Ohio Colleges Built a Network of Basic Needs Centers
abstract: ABSTRACT Across Ohio, colleges and universities have united to strategically address the basic needs challenges faced by their students. Supported by a federal grant and directed by a statewide nonprofit, several higher education administrators are tackling complex issues together through data‐driven decisions, collaborative conversations, and a shared goal of helping students persist. This article explores case studies from institutions throughout Ohio who have developed robust systems of care on their campuses and highlights how this collaboration is creating long‐term impact.

title: Legislating and Leading on Student Basic Needs: College Student Government Efforts Toward Inclusion
abstract: ABSTRACT As colleges and universities respond to students’ basic needs, structures and resources such as food pantries, emergency scholarships, housing access, transportation accommodations, mental and physical health efforts, and more become mechanisms for support. One additional structure to respond to and support students’ basic needs is a campus student government. Student governments often act as the voice of the student body to administrators and community members (Goodman 2021; Goodman and Licata‐Hoang 2023; Miller et al. 2006; Patrick 2023; Templeton et al. 2018), and addresses various issues associated with students’ needs (Goodman et al. 2021; Houze 2021). From campaigning to governing, student government leaders across the United States focus intently on how their advocacy efforts can support student access to fundamental necessities (Goodman et al. 2023). This article illuminates student governments’ role in addressing students’ basic needs. Institutions are called on to listen to and support student government leaders through legislation in the form of decision‐making, and leadership in the form of student leaders’ work and advocacy efforts.

title: Creating Healthy Options and Building Community: A Campus‐Based Intervention to Address Food Insecurity at the University of Georgia
abstract: ABSTRACT This article showcases the Let All the Big Dawgs Eat Food Scholarship program, founded in 2014, to help address student hunger at the University of Georgia. Using an exploratory qualitative research method, we conducted interviews with 14 former recipients of the food scholarship to explore their experiences and perceptions of the benefits they received from this program. Authors identified four themes from interviews with food scholarship recipients: (1) alleviation of stress due to financial constraints; (2) opportunities to build community; (3) access to healthy choices and food options; and (4) food access as a strategy that influenced academic success. We discuss key findings, implications for similar basic needs programs, and lessons learned from the Let All the Big Dawgs Eat Food Scholarship program.

title: Transforming a Campus Community: A Model for Translating Basic Needs Research Into Action
abstract: ABSTRACT This article describes how an interdisciplinary team of scholars, practitioners, and students at Rutgers University‐New Brunswick use research to inform the creation of innovative efforts to address basic needs insecurity among students. Findings from a university‐wide survey are presented followed by a description of how these research findings informed the creation of four unique programmatic initiatives.

title: Innovative Approaches to Meet College Students’ Basic Housing Needs
abstract: ABSTRACT In this article, we discuss how housing insecurity affects millions of students at institutions across the United States. We use practical examples from our own universities to show how practitioners can implement programs that help students find and secure housing. We highlight innovative on‐ and off‐campus approaches. Campus‐community partnerships are instrumental in confronting housing insecurity to improve students’ retention and graduation. We offer recommendations for staff and faculty to ensure students have a place where they belong.

title: Meeting the Basic Needs of International Students
abstract: ABSTRACT Following the COVID‐19 pandemic, many International Student Services offices are exploring and expanding the ways in which they support the basic needs of students, from food, housing, transportation, childcare, health care to mental health and wellbeing to financial assistance. In this article, three seasoned international education administrators, well‐versed in international student concerns, address some unique characteristics and challenges experienced by this population as well as innovative ideas and services they have implemented to address basic needs.

title: Ensuring Students’ Human Rights Requires Effective Assessment, Evaluation, and Research: A Call to Action
abstract: ABSTRACT Students’ basic needs—including access to food, housing, healthcare, childcare, and transportation—are fundamental human rights and essential for their success in higher education. Yet, large numbers of college students experience unmet basic needs, disproportionately impacting students who have been historically and systematically marginalized and undermining educational equity. We argue that addressing students’ basic needs is not a matter of charity or institutional benevolence, but of justice. Drawing from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and public health frameworks, we call for a systematic and equity‐centered approach to Assessment, Evaluation, and Research (AER) in higher education basic needs initiatives and present four interconnected calls to action: (1) systematic monitoring of students’ basic needs at institutional, state, and federal levels; (2) rigorous evaluation and research of programs and policies to identify effective interventions; (3) sustained investment in AER infrastructure to institutionalize evidence‐based practice; and (4) using AER to advance equity and promote justice. title: Addressing Basic Needs Barriers to Promote Student Retention, Progression, and Completion: Practices at Diverse Institutional Types
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how three institutions address college students’ basic needs insecurity and its impact on academic success. Institutional data demonstrates how case management, food access initiatives, public benefits navigation, and emergency funding address unmet basic needs that support retention, persistence, and graduation rates. The article provides further guidance on how systematic data collection and collaboration can strengthen basic needs programming and better support diverse student populations.

title: Hunger Free Higher Ed: A Statewide Approach to Food Security in Alabama
abstract: ABSTRACT This article presents Hunger Free Higher Ed (HFHE), an initiative to address food insecurity among college students in Alabama. Through a six‐step, iterative process (Engage, Assess, Plan, Implement, Evaluate, and Celebrate), HFHE supports 30 two‐ and four‐year institutions in building sustainable campus coalitions, collecting data, and implementing targeted interventions. HFHE emphasizes collaboration, data‐informed planning, and systemic change, with outcomes including improved food pantry infrastructure, increased awareness, and partnerships with food banks. HFHE's model demonstrates a scalable approach to improving student well‐being and success through coordinated institutional action.

title: Community–Campus Partnerships for Student Basic Needs
abstract: ABSTRACT Although much of the literature on community–university partnerships is about experiential learning (e.g., service‐learning) or research (e.g., community‐engaged scholarship), this article explores community–campus partnerships for supporting students’ basic needs. The need for these partnerships is vital, as the number of college students experiencing food and/or housing insecurity while obtaining their degree(s) continues to increase. Following a review of relevant literature, we share several examples of these community–campus partnerships in action. We conclude the article with a set of considerations for higher education institutions that wish to develop successful and lasting community–campus partnerships.

title: College Focused Rapid Rehousing: An Integrated Approach to Student Housing Insecurity
abstract: ABSTRACT Housing insecurity and homelessness have serious consequences for college students, including barriers to academic success, positive mental health, and the ability to achieve a college education. To address this, the 2019 California Budget Act (AB 74) provided ongoing funding to university and college campuses in the state to create and implement College Focused Rapid Rehousing (CFRR) programs. A three‐year evaluation of the statewide CFRR program, led by the Center for Equitable Higher Education (CEHE), illustrated that access to housing and supportive CFRR staff positively impacted students’ academics, mental and physical health. Yet, concerns about long‐term housing stability remained due to the current housing market. Ultimately, the CFRR evaluation showed that a partnership between community‐based housing agencies and college campuses can be a collaborative and integrative model to address student housing insecurity.

title: Better Together: Academic and Cocurricular Partnerships to Address Student Basic Needs
abstract: ABSTRACT A lack of access to basic needs is a concern for some college students, which can negatively impact retention, engagement, and overall success. To support these students, higher education administrators, staff, and faculty must find ways to work together across divisions to promote collaborative solutions. In this article, we discuss the history of academic and co‐curricular partnerships, describe a unique case study with examples of basic needs partnerships between academics and student affairs at one institution, and provide recommendations for collaboration.

title: Beyond Funding: The Transformative Role of Indigenous Scholarship Providers in U.S. Higher Education
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the evolving role of Indigenous scholarship providers in the United States, highlighting their critical contributions to educational equity, Tribal sovereignty, and student success. Grounded in a decolonizing framework and informed by Indigenous paradigms of relationality, reciprocity, and responsibility, the article explores how organizations such as the Cobell Scholarship Program, American Indian College Fund, Native Forward Scholars Fund, and AISES—Advancing Indigenous People in STEM extend beyond financial aid to offer culturally affirming support systems for Native college students. Through historical analysis, contemporary case studies, and emerging practices in Indigenous data sovereignty, the article illustrates how these providers address the systemic challenges facing American Indian and Alaska Native students in both Tribal and non‐Tribal institutions. The authors offer policy recommendations and strategic insights for student affairs professionals and higher education leaders seeking to better support Native learners. By centering Indigenous voices and worldviews, the article advocates for a transformative shift in how scholarship and stud

title: “Our Sea of Islands”: Mapping Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander Students Success
abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides an overview of the Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander (NHPI) community, focusing on historical, cultural, and social realities which shape NHPI student experiences. Authors review existing research on NHPI students, highlight curricular and co‐curricular activities targeting NHPI student success, and conclude by offering strategies that educators may consider to support NHPI students.

title: National Native Scholarship Providers as Research and Data Partners: A Case Study in Advancing Evidence‐Based Support for Indigenous College Student Outcomes
abstract: ABSTRACT American Indian and Alaska Native students remain largely invisible in national higher education research datasets, limiting institutions’ ability to design effective recruitment, retention, and completion strategies. In response, the four largest Native scholarship organizations in the United States — the Cobell Scholarship Program, American Indian College Fund, AISES, and Native Forward — formed the National Native Scholarship Providers (NNSP), a collaborative research and data partnership addressing evidence gaps in Indigenous college access, affordability, belonging, and persistence. This article presents a case study of NNSP's interorganizational research collaboration. The consortium's first national mixed‐methods study examined Indigenous college affordability with participation from all four organizations. Subsequent sense of belonging and campus climate research was conducted through partnership among the Cobell Scholarship Program, AISES, and the College Fund, illustrating an adaptive collaboration model responsive to organizational capacity and evolving research priorities. Across studies, NNSP employs nationally representative surveys and Indigenous qualitative

title: Introduction to Indigenous Student Affairs
abstract: ABSTRACT Indigenous Student Affairs (ISA) has grown from community‐driven advocacy into a vital support space within higher education. This article, written in a narrative style and grounded in a conversation among four ISA educators, traces the history and literature of ISA, highlights practitioners’ lived experiences across diverse institutional contexts, and identifies implications and future directions for sustaining ISA units, professionals, and communities.

title: In the Arctic: Serving the Alaska Native Iñupiaq Students Arctic‐mi: Ikayuġniq IñupiatIḷisaqtuatigun Alaska‐mi
abstract: ABSTRACT In this article, the author shares observations about serving the Alaska Native students on the North Slope at the only Tribal College in Alaska. The institution's #1 priority in its strategic plan is to indigenize the campus in every way possible.

title: Editors’ Notes
What Matters to Us?: Contemplating a Holistic Indigenous Identity Framework Through Four Framing Questions
abstract: ABSTRACT This article introduces a conceptual framework for Indigenous college student identity development, addressing the limitations of mainstream student development theories rooted in Western, Eurocentric worldviews. Drawing on Tribal Critical Race Theory and relationality, we propose four guiding questions—Where are we? Who are we? Who am I responsible to? How do we know what we know?—to illuminate the intersecting cultural, historical, and social complexities shaping Native students’ identities.

title: Advocating for Native‐Centric Financial Aid: Lessons From the Native Student Aid Portal
abstract: ABSTRACT Native‐centric financial aid is an essential tool promoting college access and success for Native American students and a component of Native nation building. Yet, a small but growing body of literature indicates existing financial aid opportunities do not fully meet the lived realities of Native students. This article offers insights from the Native Student Aid Portal about the characteristics of Native‐centric financial aid at the institutional, postsecondary system, and state levels. We close by highlighting key lessons learned that inform student service professionals’ efforts to advance Native student services, with an emphasis on how improving financial aid information emerged as an essential strategy.

title: Indigenous Student Affairs Professional Networks in Higher Education Associations
abstract: ABSTRACT Professional higher education associations offer knowledge, support, and networking for professionals. This chapter examines five national affinity groups, highlighting their efforts to enhance Native and Indigenous student success. We discuss their challenges, opportunities, contributions, and future aspirations for supporting the profession and strengthening community across higher education.

title: Foreword
“Many Buds Blooming”: Lived Experience and Insights From Native American Graduate Students
abstract: ABSTRACT Native American graduate students have a unique experience in higher education from their peers and from Native undergraduate students. This article highlights the challenges and triumphs of 12 Native American graduate students, focusing on their unique cultural perspectives and systemic obstacles they encounter in graduate education. Through their narratives, the article offers insights into their experiences, resilience, and the importance of cultural and academic support, providing guidance for faculty, staff, and future Native American graduate scholars.

title: “Letting Them Know They Are Part of the Family”: Developing Native American Alumni Engagement in Higher Education
abstract: ABSTRACT This article explores the creation of a Native alumni engagement network, position, and legacy at the University of South Dakota. Through archival review, contemporary research, and first person experience by the researchers, this article examines the significance of a position focused on Native alumni engagement and the need for higher education's investment in Native alumni's triumphs, challenges, and contributions. By investing in alumni engagement, institutions also invest in Native student recruitment, persistence, retention, and mentorship.

title: RESOURCES
Missing the Mark: Native American Student Involvement in Leadership Development Experiences
abstract: ABSTRACT Using data drawn from the Multi‐Institutional Study of Leadership (MSL), the authors found that Native American college students’ participation in leadership development experiences was low. Those who participated in leadership development experiences most often did so in short‐term, often one‐off experiences. The relationship between participation and leadership self‐efficacy (LSE) and leadership capacity were examined. Recommendations for enhancing Native American student involvement in leadership development experiences are provided to address leadership practices within institutions of higher education.

title: Afterword
Future Issues in Student Affairs and Higher Education
abstract: ABSTRACT US higher education is undergoing rapid change, faster than it has in its 400‐year history. While some changes could have been predicted, others, such as COVID, could not. This article will explore issues in the future of higher education, implications for student affairs, and their impact on the preparation of higher education graduate professionals.

title: Prior and Current Professional Association Influences on Graduate Preparation Programs
abstract: ABSTRACT Professional associations support a field in many ways, including professionalization, setting standards of practice, advocating for members and the industry it supports, and generating and sharing knowledge, research, and scholarship. While they provide ongoing education, they can play a more intentional role in professional preparation. This article will discuss how comprehensive and functional area professional associations can support preparation for entry into the field of student affairs and higher education.

title: The Future of Professional Preparation
abstract: ABSTRACT In this final article, we have been tasked with discussing the future of professional preparation in student affairs. Making predictions about the future of anything, even in sedentary times, is dicey, so given the dynamism and chaos of today's world, the reader will find no such forecasts here. Instead, we summarize the challenges facing the field vis‐a‐vis professional preparation, and we propose a series of possible actions to be considered by the field in order to meet those challenges. Our call to the field is to design and shape the future of professional preparation, not to just let the default future happen.

title: Editors’ Notes
Leading for Change in Higher Education Through Student Affairs Professional Preparation at the Master's Level
abstract: ABSTRACT Master's programs serve as a traditional entry point for many professionals working in higher education. These programs are at an inflection point with declining enrollments, financial constraints at institutions negatively impacting graduate assistantships, proliferation of anti‐diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice (DEIJ) policies, and different pathways into the field. This article invites readers into a critical and reflective conversation about four contemporary key issues impacting graduate programs and key collaborators (i.e., program faculty, campus partners, and graduate students).

title: Professional Preparation, Ongoing Learning, and Credentialing
abstract: ABSTRACT Some of the first competencies for higher education professionals were published in the 1937 Student Personnel Point of View by the American Council on Education. These have evolved and expanded over time, and professional associations have defined knowledge, skills, and dispositions for the field in general and specific functional areas. These competencies, along with relevant ethical guidelines, professional standards, and learning opportunities hosted by professional organizations provide a framework for learners across a continuum encompassing a foundation of preparing future professionals through continuous learning and professional development. Recently, professional credentialing in the forms of certificates and certification was introduced as a voluntary means to further validate professionals’ knowledge and incentivize continued learning.

title: History and Current State of Doctoral Preparation Programs
abstract: ABSTRACT Higher education and student affairs (HESA) doctoral programs might not be keeping pace in preparing leaders for the challenging roles they will occupy in the future. Curricula may lack relevance to leadership practice, and doctoral programs might emphasize research excellence and preparing future faculty over leadership development and administrative career paths. Previous efforts to make HESA graduate programs more relevant to leadership practice have focused on the development of standards or guidelines. But that approach relies on a static document to address a fluid problem. The complexities of postsecondary leadership suggest the need for a fluid and ongoing process of leadership development, where faculty and doctoral students can learn about and practice leadership in real‐time in response to emerging challenges in the field. This article explains how HESA doctoral programs can create dynamic feedback loops that generate real‐time learning about leadership. As these feedback loops generate new knowledge about leadership, HESA program faculty can incorporate these insights into the curriculum, learning environment, and research experiences for doctoral students.

title: How Changing Student Demographics Shape and Shift the Future of the Profession: Implications for Student Affairs Professional Preparation
abstract: ABSTRACT The demographic landscape of higher education is shifting , undergoing a profound transformation, with “new majority” student populations—such as first‐generation students, ethnic minorities, individuals with disabilities, veterans, and returning adults—becoming increasingly prevalent. This article explores the implications of these shifts for the preparation of future higher education and student affairs professionals, emphasizing the need for graduate training and professional development that addresses the diverse and intersecting identities of today's students. Grounded in an intersectional framework, the article examines the unique challenges and opportunities these students face and highlights strategies for enhancing the preparation of future professionals who would be well‐equipped to foster equity, belonging, and success for all students in higher education. By focusing on inclusive practices and forward‐thinking approaches, this article contributes to existing scholarship while offering a vision for a more responsive and student‐centered future in higher education.

title: Professional Competencies for the Future of Student Affairs
abstract: ABSTRACT Some of the first competencies for higher education professionals were published in the 1937 Student Personnel Point of View . These have evolved and expanded over time, and professional associations have defined knowledge, skills, and dispositions for the field in general and specific functional areas. These competencies, along with the CAS standards for Master's Level Higher Education and Student Affairs Professional Preparation Programs , provide the foundation for preparing future practitioners.

title: The Power and Importance of Reciprocity in Community‐Engaged Research: Centering College Students’ Beliefs
abstract: ABSTRACT This article explores how college students’ beliefs about reciprocity are shaped through community engagement, particularly in the context of community‐engaged research. Recent studies highlight the central role of reciprocity in students’ engagement experiences; students not only seek reciprocal relationships and meaningful impact, but also define community engagement through this lens. Drawing on vignettes co‐authored by undergraduate researchers, this chapter illustrates how reciprocity functions in practice. The vignettes focus on students’ participation in an undergraduate research collaborative that examines how higher education institutions can foster more equitable and sustained relationships with the neighborhoods and communities that host them. Key takeaways from each vignette offer insights for designing and implementing more equitable approaches to community‐engaged teaching, learning, and research.
